title: The 'Wild West' of AI in Schools: A Chatbot Named Jordan and a $78,650 Experiment
summary:
In Dayton, Ohio, a small group of students at an alternative school spent part of last year talking every morning with an AI chatbot named Jordan. Unlike typical chatbots designed to be agreeable, Jordan acts angsty. On the day NPR visited, Jordan told students: "Lately, I've been feeling like what's the point of any of this? I'm not failing. I just don't care. You ever feel like that?"

One sophomore, identified only as K, said he built a relationship with the chatbot. "I don't really see it as like an AI on a computer. It's Jordan — like, I'm texting somebody," he said. K added that answering Jordan every morning helped him "solve my own problems."

Dayton Public Schools paid the ed tech company SchoolAI $72,600 last academic year for multiple AI tools, including Jordan. The district renewed the contract this year for $78,650. Administrators say they want to see whether Jordan helps students open up about their emotions, information that could be useful for school therapists. Families and students were notified that chat logs could be viewed by school employees, an external evaluator and SchoolAI staff.

Across the U.S., schools are experimenting with AI in many ways: developing lesson plans, tracking student progress, giving feedback on work, and even introducing an AI-powered humanoid robot at a San Diego charter school. "It feels very Wild West in terms of the randomness," says Robin Lake, director of the Center on Reinventing Public Education.

But research is scarce. A Stanford University review of more than 800 academic papers found extremely limited evidence on how schools can use AI to help students and avoid harms. Some studies suggest carefully designed AI tools show more promise than general-purpose chatbots. There is also no consensus on how to measure what works. "We need state and federal leadership," Lake says.

Dayton Superintendent David Lawrence defended the experiment. "When the history is written, it'll say that 'Hey, they were really cutting-edge, innovative and ahead of the curve in the interest of children,'" he said. The district plans to continue using AI at the alternative school and may deploy more social-emotional chatbots.
why_it_matters: AI tools are spreading through schools far faster than the evidence about whether they help, so today's students are effectively the test subjects — the rules being written now about privacy, data and what a chatbot should say to a teenager will shape how a whole generation learns.

background_read: Dayton is a mid-sized city in Ohio, and SchoolAI is a company that sells AI tools — including the chatbot Jordan — to school districts.

NPR (National Public Radio, a nonprofit U.S. news network funded partly by the public) reported the Dayton story. General-purpose AI chatbots became widely available to students in late 2022, when ChatGPT launched, and schools have argued ever since about whether to ban them or use them.
Stanford University (a major research university in California) reviewed more than 800 academic papers and found little solid evidence about AI's effects in classrooms.

Student privacy in the U.S. is protected by laws such as FERPA (the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act), which requires schools to keep education records private — a rule that gets complicated when a private company's staff can read what students type.
Because there is no national standard for AI in schools, districts like Dayton make these decisions largely on their own, which is why contracts and rules vary so much from place to place.

perspectives.description: Administrators say the goal is to learn whether Jordan helps students open up about their emotions, information school therapists could use. Student K says the daily chats helped him work through his own problems, describing Jordan almost like a friend rather than software.

Families were told that chat logs could be viewed by school employees, an outside evaluator and SchoolAI staff, which means deeply personal messages may sit with a company. A Stanford review of more than 800 papers found extremely limited evidence that any of this helps students or avoids harm.

This fits a familiar pattern: schools adopt new technology faster than evidence and regulation can keep up, from filmstrips to laptops to chatbots. Robin Lake's 'Wild West' image captures a market where vendors sell many tools and nobody can yet say which ones work.

Lake argues that states and the federal government need to set standards for measuring results and protecting student data. Without them, districts will keep making costly, uneven bets — like Dayton's renewed $78,650 contract — and students will keep being the experiment.
